title: Polynomials

findings.finding: The instruction names coefficient comparison but does not explain the principle needed to form the equations.
findings.breakdown: Knowing what a coefficient is does not establish why equivalence requires matching coefficients separately, including coefficients of powers absent from one side.
findings.checked: p4-formal-definition identifies coefficients; p7-q12 constrains named coefficients but does not compare identities. p7-q13 supplies the method's name without explaining its decisive step.
findings.assumptions: Expansion and simultaneous linear equations are prior algebra skills. Coefficient comparison is new in the supplied teaching.

repair.proposal: Append to p7-q13's instruction: “Equivalent polynomial expressions have equal coefficients of matching powers of x. After expanding and collecting terms, equate these coefficients separately; a missing power has coefficient zero.”

findings.doneWhen: Students have an explicit reason for forming separate coefficient equations in both parts.

findings.finding: A controlled run would expose how leading-term cancellation changes degree before the existing degree questions.
findings.breakdown: The existing calculated parts retain their maximum degree; part e then asks students to consider cancellation.
findings.checked: All proposed expansions and degrees are correct. The run changes only Q's leading coefficient and uses operations taught in this topic.
findings.assumptions: This is one of four retained suggestions.

repair.proposal: After p11-q1-c, before the degree questions, add: “Predict the degree before expanding.” Under the existing sum-and-difference instruction, use P(x)=2x²+x+1 throughout: (i) Q(x)=x²+3x+4: sum 3x²+4x+5, difference x²−2x−3, both degree 2; (ii) Q(x)=2x²+3x+4: sum 4x²+4x+5, degree 2; difference −2x−3, degree 1; (iii) Q(x)=−2x²+3x+4: sum 4x+5, degree 1; difference 4x²−2x−3, degree 2. Follow with an unpatterned part: P(x)=3x³−x+2 and Q(x)=−3x³+2x²+5: sum 2x²−x+7, degree 2; difference 6x³−2x²−x−3, degree 3.

findings.doneWhen: The run supplies a numerical comparison of cancellation while preserving the existing degree questions.

findings.finding: p21-q2-a requires repeated-root behaviour before that behaviour is taught.
findings.breakdown: Correct factorisation gives x²(x+2)(x+1), but preceding sketching instruction does not explain why the graph touches rather than crosses at zero.
findings.checked: p17 shows tangencies without connecting them to multiplicity. p19 models simple roots. The required explanation and worked examples appear in the following topic at p22–p23.
findings.assumptions: Repeated-root graphing is new within this booklet.

repair.proposal: Move p21-q2-a to immediately after the p23 worked examples, retaining its instruction to factorise before sketching.

findings.doneWhen: Students encounter this double-root sketch after the existing multiplicity teaching.

findings.finding: The graphing topic does not rehearse solving factored equations before using the null-factor law.
findings.breakdown: The worked sketch lists roots directly. Students whose recall of setting factors equal to zero is weak receive no opening check of that substantial prerequisite.
findings.checked: The topic has no review. p16 rehearses products and p18 rehearses end behaviour. The preceding operations topic does not practise solving factored equations. p19 names the null-factor law but does not rebuild its use.
findings.assumptions: The null-factor law and solving linear equations are prior course knowledge. Calculator access does not affect this finding.

repair.proposal: Add three short opening items: (a) Solve (x−2)(x+3)=0. (b) Solve x(x−4)=0. (c) Solve (2x−3)(5−x)=0. Answers: (a) 2, −3; (b) 0, 4; (c) 3/2, 5. Keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: The teacher can check recall of solving factored equations before the worked sketch.

findings.finding: Compare polynomials with the same intercepts and end directions but different root multiplicities.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up isolates the local behaviour that intercept locations alone do not determine.
findings.checked: The quadratic 2(x−1)(x+1) has roots −1 and 1 and y-intercept −2. It crosses ordinarily at both roots; the existing graph has triple, flattened crossings. These distinctions are taught at p22–p24.
findings.assumptions: This is one of four retained suggestions.

repair.proposal: Add to p30-q9: (c) Find a quadratic polynomial with roots −1 and 1 and y-intercept −2. Answer: y=2(x−1)(x+1). (d) Describe how its graph differs from the graph in part b at these roots. Answer: the quadratic crosses without flattening at both roots; part b has flattened crossings at both.

findings.doneWhen: The optional follow-up compares ordinary and flattened crossings using the existing graph's numbers.

findings.finding: Polynomial long division begins without rehearsing the symbolic operations needed in each cycle.
findings.breakdown: Students must learn the division cycle while retrieving monomial division, distribution and subtraction of signed polynomial terms.
findings.checked: p32 reviews division terminology only. Distribution and polynomial subtraction were taught in the operations topic, with graphing and multiplicity intervening. The immediately preceding topic does not rehearse these operations.
findings.assumptions: Students perform symbolic manipulation themselves; calculator availability does not remove this prerequisite.

repair.proposal: Before p33-polynomial-division-theory, add: (a) Simplify 3x²÷x and 8x³÷2x. (b) Expand 3x(x−1). (c) Expand −8(x−1). (d) Simplify (3x²−11x+2)−(3x²−3x). Answers: (a) 3x, 4x²; (b) 3x²−3x; (c) −8x+8; (d) −8x+2. Keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: These prerequisite operations are checked before the first polynomial long-division example.

findings.finding: The division teaching omits the stopping decision before its first nonconstant remainder.
findings.breakdown: The instruction to divide leading terms does not tell students why they should stop at −4x+4 rather than attempt −4x÷x².
findings.checked: p33 examples stop at constants without stating the criterion. p39 stops at a linear remainder. The explicit degree restriction appears at p41, after this example.
findings.assumptions: Polynomial long division is new in this topic.

repair.proposal: Append to p33-polynomial-division-theory: “Stop when the remainder is zero or has lower degree than the divisor.” At p39-example-step4 add: “The remainder −4x+4 has degree 1, below the divisor's degree 2, so stop.”

findings.doneWhen: The stopping rule is available from the first division and explicitly applied to the nonconstant remainder.

findings.finding: Two division tasks are repeated unchanged without an explicit retrieval or comparison purpose.
findings.breakdown: p36-q2-e repeats p34-d, and p38-q4-e repeats p37-q3-a. Each pair has identical dividends, divisors and required results.
findings.checked: Compared complete prompts and enclosing instructions. Fraction notation in p36-q2-e does not change the division task. Both proposed replacement identities expand correctly.
findings.assumptions: No explicit instructional purpose justifies either repeated whole task.

repair.proposal: Replace p36-q2-e with (4x³−4x²+9x+13)/(2x+1). Answer: 2x²−3x+6+7/(2x+1). Replace p38-q4-e with (x³−7x+4)÷(x−2). Answer: x²+2x−3−2/(x−2). Retain the earlier copies.

findings.doneWhen: Both later copies retain their task structure with different values and the stated answers.

findings.finding: Varying only the dividend's constant term would expose its effect on the remainder.
findings.breakdown: The run connects changes to a dividend with an unchanged quotient and a corresponding change in remainder.
findings.checked: Every proposed identity expands correctly. Division and quotient-remainder notation are available by this topic; the added instruction is one prediction line.
findings.assumptions: This is one of four retained suggestions.

repair.proposal: Immediately after p42-q3-a, add under the existing instruction: “Predict which part of your answer will change.” (i) (x³+x²−2x)÷(x−1); answer: x³+x²−2x=(x−1)(x²+2x). (ii) (x³+x²−2x+1)÷(x−1); answer: x³+x²−2x+1=(x−1)(x²+2x)+1. (iii) (x³+x²−2x−2)÷(x−1); answer: x³+x²−2x−2=(x−1)(x²+2x)−2. Follow with an unpatterned part: (x³+2x²−x+4)÷(x+1); answer: x³+2x²−x+4=(x+1)(x²+x−2)+6. Only the constant term varies in the run.

findings.doneWhen: The optional run varies one feature and concludes with an unpatterned division.

findings.finding: The complete solving example combines earlier methods without rehearsing quadratic factorisation and solving a factored equation.
findings.breakdown: Students can find an integer root and divide successfully but still break down when factorising the quotient or extracting solutions.
findings.checked: p59 rehearses root testing. Earlier quotient-remainder practice uses quadratic factorisation, and graphing uses the null-factor law, but neither is rehearsed before this combined solving example.
findings.assumptions: Quadratic factorisation and the null-factor law are prior course knowledge. Calculator access does not affect the finding.

repair.proposal: Immediately before p60-teaching, add three short review items: (a) Factorise x²+x−12. (b) Factorise 2x²−7x+3. (c) Solve (x+4)(2x−3)=0. Answers: (a) (x+4)(x−3); (b) (2x−1)(x−3); (c) x=−4 or 3/2. Keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: Students rehearse quadratic factorisation and the null-factor law before combining them with root testing and division.

findings.finding: Use the existing factorisation to connect polynomial solving with repeated-root graphing.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up distinguishes a repeated real zero from a quadratic factor with no real zeroes.
findings.checked: (x−2)²(x²+3x+3) expands to the given polynomial. The quadratic factor is always positive, so 2 is the only real zero and the graph touches there. The y-intercept is 12 and both ends rise. All required methods occur earlier.
findings.assumptions: This is one of four retained suggestions.

repair.proposal: Add a follow-up to p70-q23: “Hence sketch y=x⁴−x³−5x²+12, marking its intercepts.” Expected answer: both ends rise; y-intercept (0,12); the only x-intercept is (2,0), where the graph touches the axis and turns upwards.

findings.doneWhen: The optional sketch uses the factorisation already obtained.

contextQuestions.question: Before this booklet, have students learned the defining relationships for even and odd functions, P(−x)=P(x) and P(−x)=−P(x)? These definitions are absent from the supplied teaching; their prior availability determines whether p14-q10 and p14-q11 need a teaching cue.

protectedGroups.observation: The same product connects the area model to symbolic distribution.
protectedGroups.varies: Representation and organisation of the products.
protectedGroups.invariant: Both factors and the resulting polynomial.

protectedGroups.observation: Reusing the investigated product models the transition from a nine-cell grid to algebraic working.
protectedGroups.invariant: Factors and all nine pairwise products.

protectedGroups.observation: Reversing operand order exposes commutativity of addition and multiplication and its failure for subtraction.
Changing leading coefficients changes the leading term while unchanged factor constants preserve the constant term until the overall sign changes.
protectedGroups.varies: One coefficient at a time, then the overall sign.

protectedGroups.observation: Changing a second x coefficient to negative reverses the leading-term sign without changing the constant term.
protectedGroups.varies: The sign of the x term in the last factor.

protectedGroups.observation: A numerical multiplier changes the leading coefficient while the zero constant term remains zero.
protectedGroups.invariant: Roots, repeated factor, degree and zero constant term.

protectedGroups.observation: Changing one root's multiplicity reveals crossing, bouncing and flattened contact while preserving the root locations.
protectedGroups.varies: One factor exponent at each step.
protectedGroups.invariant: Root locations -3, 1 and 2, and leading coefficient 1.

protectedGroups.observation: Adding a simple root at zero changes degree parity and the left-end direction while retaining the existing roots and their multiplicities.
Changing the divisor changes both quotient and remainder, and one choice gives exact division.
protectedGroups.varies: The constant term of the monic linear divisor; completion support also varies.
protectedGroups.invariant: Dividend x²+9x+18 and the long-division method.

protectedGroups.observation: Opposite-sign inputs of the same magnitude can produce different factor decisions.
protectedGroups.varies: The sign within each pair, then the magnitude across pairs.
protectedGroups.invariant: The polynomial and the factor-testing method.

protectedGroups.observation: The final pair contrasts evaluation at 2 and -2: even-power terms keep their signs while the odd-power term changes sign.
protectedGroups.varies: The divisor, including the sign of the input in the last two parts.
protectedGroups.invariant: The polynomial x^4-x^3+3x^2 and the remainder-theorem method.

protectedGroups.observation: An unknown coefficient can occupy different terms without changing the method of equating the evaluated polynomial to the stated remainder.
protectedGroups.varies: The position of k, the divisor and the stated remainder.
protectedGroups.invariant: One unknown coefficient and one linear equation after substitution.

protectedGroups.observation: The same leading-term and constant-term reasoning determines a remaining factor when one known factor becomes non-monic.
protectedGroups.varies: Monic versus non-monic supplied linear factors.
protectedGroups.invariant: Two established factors of a cubic and the instruction to infer the third from coefficients.

protectedGroups.observation: A remaining quadratic can contribute two additional real solutions or none.
protectedGroups.varies: The sign of the quadratic discriminant.
protectedGroups.invariant: A supplied linear factor times a quadratic, solved using the null factor law and quadratic formula.
